preamble: Raising of the mid central vowel [ə] to the close central vowel [ɨ]. In Sundanese, Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *ə became the vowel written eu, /ɨ/, which contrasts with a separate /ə/ written e: PMP *ləŋən 'forearm' > leungeun 'hand', PWMP *qasəp 'smoke' > haseup /haˈsɨp/. Many common words have e /ə/ for PMP *ə instead, such as gənəp 'six' (PWMP *gənəp 'complete; even') and təŋah 'half' (PMP *təŋaq). The Austronesian Comparative Dictionary, following Nothofer (1975), takes /ə/ in place of /ɨ/ as a sign of borrowing, but suggests that a group of native words, including much or all of the onomatopoeic vocabulary, also kept /ə/: PWMP *qiəm₁ 'animal sound' gives hiem '(of a horse) to neigh', while PWMP *qiəm₂ 'shade, darkness' gives hiɨm 'shade, shadow'. The realization of eu differs by speaker and region, written [ɨ], [ɤ] (Bandung), [ɯ] (Tangerang) or [ɘ]; the atlas writes ɨ. In Romanian, Latin stressed a before /n/ or before /m/ plus a consonant became /ɨ/ (written â, î): campus > câmp, lāna > lână, quando > când. Renwick (2012), following Rosetti, gives the path as a > ă > ɨ, with the ă stage reconstructed only (*cămp, *lănă), and Wikipedia's History of the Romanian language (after Sala 2012) describes the same two steps as part of a wider pre-nasal raising that also gave bene > bine and nomen > nume. Renwick writes ă as /ʌ/; the atlas files it as ə, as in casă [ˈka.sə].

examples.to: Sundanese leungeun 'hand', with eu /ɨ/ in both syllables
Sundanese tɨlɨm 'go under water, plunge in'

examples.from: Latin campus 'field', with stressed a raised to ă before the nasal
examples.note: Renwick (2012) reconstructs the intermediate *cămp; no form with ă is attested. The rule raises stressed ă before /n/ or /m/ plus a consonant.

examples.from: Latin lāna 'wool', with stressed a raised to ă before the nasal
Latin quando 'when', with stressed a raised to ă before the nasal
